ABSTRACT 
This study was to investigate the effects of bacterial cellulose (BC), konjac glucomannan 
(KGM) and combined BC/KGM fiber supplementations on high-fat (HF) diet-induced obesity 
in C57BL/6J mice. The results showed that combined BC/KGM supplementation in HF-fed 
mice was more efficient in reducing body weight, lowing serum lipid profits and suppressing 
insulin resistance than single BC or KGM. Meanwhile, supplementation with combined 
BC/KGM fiber could attenuate more efficiently the HF-diet induced liver injury via decreasing 
hepatic steatosis in comparison with only BC or KGM supplementation. Furthermore, combined 
BC/KGM fiber supplementation in HF-fed mice had more positive effect on obesity-associated 
hepatic inflammation through reducing TNF-α and IL-6 levels and suppressing protein 
expression level of Nrf-2/ARE as compared with BC or KGM alone. Consumption of the 
dietary fibers, especially the mixed BC/KGM, exhibited an improved antioxidant defense 
system and reduced liver lipid peroxidation through increasing the activity of antioxidant 
enzymes and reducing MDA formation in the liver. Moreover, this fiber supplementation 
regulated the levels of leptin and adiponectin, and inhibited the protein expressions of PPARγ by 
reducing the size of cells in adipose tissue of HF diet-fed mice. Therefore, fiber supplementation 
(especially the combined BC/KGM) efficiently inhibited HF-induced obesity in mice through 
attenuating insulin resistance, liver injury and inflammation, and enhancing antioxidant defense 
system and regulating the secretion of adipocytokines and adipogenesis-associated proteins. 
Keywords: bacterial cellulose; konjac glucomannan; anti-obesity; hepatic steatosis; 
inflammation; oxidant stress

Introduction 
Hepatic problems are life-threatening with high rates of mortality in the world, and many 
studies have demonstrated that a risk factor for acute liver injury is overweight or obesity. In the 
past few decades obesity has rapidly increased all around the world with increasingly high 
sugars or fat calorie food (fast food or junk food).1-6 The WHO noted that approximately 2.3 
billion adults are overweight and more than 700 million are obese.7 Generally speaking, obesity 
has been viewed as one of the most serious public health problems in the 21st century and 
classified as a disease by the American Medical Association since 2013.8 Herein, reduction of 
energy intake or increase of basal metabolic rate has been simplistically regarded as a 
therapeutic solution for controlling body weight gain.9 However, many researches have 
demonstrated that sufficient consumption of dietary fibers is able to control body weight, thus 
promoting beneficial physiological functions including attenuation of blood lipid, cholesterol 
and cardiovascular diseases.10 
Dietary fibers (DFs) are the indigestible portion of food, which can be divided into soluble 
and insoluble fiber. DFs as the soluble part are able to be fermented to yield short-chain fatty 
acids in the colon, which are beneficial to lipid metabolism, cardiovascular disease prevention, 
mucosal differentiation or apoptosis, and mucosal barrier function.11, 12 For the insoluble part it 
also has a generally low fermentability, but it possesses passive hygroscopic properties to 
increase bulk, soften stool, and shorten transit time through the intestinal tract.11, 12 Furthermore, 
DFs isolates or fiber-rich foods are beneficial to weight control through reducing energy intake 
in comparison to non-fibre-containing alternatives, reducing the amount of energy that is 
absorbed from ingested foods, increasing postprandial energy expenditure (possibly via

Nevertheless, DFs are regarded as important ingredient for the diets with regulatory authorities 
in many developed countries, recommending increases in fiber intake.14 The importance of DFs 
has encouraged a continuing search for new fiber sources for functional food application. 
However, different fiber types (e.g. inulin, beta-glucan) and/or sources (pulses, grains, etc.) have 
different physical and biological properties, which may affect metabolic health in distinct 
ways.15 Therefore, it is worth characterizing diverse fiber sources to ensure a broad range of 
options in the food supply. 
Bacterial cellulose (BC), an extremely pure natural microbe exocellular insoluble 
polysaccharide (linear homopolysaccharide composed of D-glucopyranose units linked by 
b-1,4-glycosidic bonds), has unusual properties including high purity, high crystallinity (absence 
of lignin or hemicelluloses), high degree of polymerization, high water absorbing and holding 
capacity, high tensile strength, and strong biological adaptability.16, 17 BC is more valuable than 
plant-derived cellulose although BC is identical in chemical composition to plant celluloses.18 
Consequently, BC presents a potential alternative to plant-derived cellulose for specific 
applications in bio-medicine, cosmetics, food fields, and other applications. In the Southeast 
Asia, BC is well known as traditional gel delicacy (nata) and BC has generally been recognized 
as safe (GRAS) by the USA Food and Drug Administration since 1992.19-21 Moreover, BC has 
been demonstrated as a promising low calorie bulking ingredient for the development of novel 
model DFs in functional foods.21 Taken together, BC would be a great promising DF because of 
its easy isolation and purity (free of lignin). Therefore, it is well worth studying on the 
physiological functions of BC to exploit its potential food application. Konjac glucomannan

(KGM) is a hydrophilic soluble fiber derived from the tuber of Amorphophallus konjac C. 
Koch.22 KGM has traditionally been consumed as rubbery, jelly, noodles, and other food 
products in Asia for centuries. Recently, KGM has been found to be a potential adjunct for 
obesity, glycemic control and a hypocholesterolemic reagent.23-25 KGM supplement promoted 
bowel movement by 30%.26 However, a few studies have reported the protective effects of 
KGM as a DF on the non-alcoholic fatty liver injury induced by high-fat diets.  
In the present study, we investigated the effects of different supplementations with BC, KGM 
and combined BC/KGM on chronic HF diet-induced hepatic damage in C57BL/6J mice. To 
reveal the potential mechanisms, biochemical analysis of the serum and liver was first 
performed in all the experimental mice. Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) and the serum 
glucose and insulin test were also performed. Furthermore, cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, FAS, LPL, 
ADPN and LEP) and protein expressions (Nrf-2, ARE and PPARγ) in the liver and adipose were 
determined. Finally, histological structures of representative epididymal adipose tissue and liver 
samples from the mice were observed using Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and oil red O 
staining, respectively.

Preparation of bacterial cellulose 
BC was prepared according to our previous method.18 Briefly, Komagataeibacter hansenii 
CGMCC 3917 was cultured at 30°C under static conditions in fermentation medium (pH 5.0) 
containing 2% of glucose (w/v), 0.5% of yeast extract (w/v), 0.1% of K2HPO4 (w/v), 1.5% of 
MgSO4 (w/v), 2% of ethanol (v/v). After 14 days incubation, the cellulose membrane was 
harvested and rinsed with running water overnight, soaked in 0.1 M NaOH solution at 80°C for 
30 min, and then washed with deionized water several times to completely remove alkali and

Animals and dietary treatments 
50 male C57BL/6J mice (three week-old) were obtained from the Experimental Animal 
Center of Xi’an Jiaotong University (Xi’an, China) and housed under standard condition 
maintained at room temperature of 22 ± 2°C and a relative humidity of 55 ± 5% with 12/12 h 
light-dark cycles. All mice were offered pellets of commercial chow for 1 week after arrival. 
The mice were randomly divided into five groups (n=10/group). The normal diet group was fed 
with normal diet (M01-F, SLAC laboratory Animal, Shanghai, China) providing 60.5% of 
energy as carbohydrates, 25.7% as protein, and 13.8% as fat. The high fat (HF) dietary group 
was fed with high fat diet (M04-F, SLAC laboratory Animal, Shanghai, China) providing 45% 
of energy as carbohydrates, 18.7% as protein, and 36.3% as fat. The fiber supplement was 
referred to the previous study and the recommanded nutrient intakes of dietary fiber by Food 
and Drug Administration (FDA) with modifications.14, 27 The BC dietary group was fed with 
high fat diet containing 8% BC. The KGM dietary group was fed with high fat diet containing 8% 
KGM. The BC/KGM dietary group (n=10) was fed with high fat diet containing 4% BC and 4% 
KGM. All animals were allowed free access to food and water, and their food consumption was 
monitored weekly, while their body weights were measured every two weeks during the 
experiment period. All of the experimental procedures were followed by Guide for the Care and 
Use of Laboratory Animals: Eighth Edition, ISBN-10: 0-309-15396-4, and the animal protocol

After feeding for 16 weeks, all mice were fasted for 12 h, and subsequently, the mice were 
fully anesthetized by the inhalation of isoflurane and then sacrificed to obtain blood, liver and 
adipose tissue. On the basis of the records of the body weight and corresponding liver weight of 
every mouse, we calculated the hepatosomatic index (HI) according to the following formula: 
HI% =liver weight (g) /body weight (g) × 100%. The blood samples were collected and 
centrifuged at 3000g, 37°C for 10 min. The supernatant was transferred to another PE tube and 
stored at -80°C for further biochemical analysis, and liver and abdominal adipose weight was 
measured and stored at -80°C for further analysis.  
Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) and serum glucose and insulin 
For OGTT, glucose (2 g/kg body weight) was given by gavage after 8 h of fasting, and plasma 
glucose levels were measured using an OneTouch Ultra glucometer (Lifescan Benelux, Beerse, 
Belgium) at 15, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min after the injection. 28 Besides, the homeostatic model 
assessment (HOMA) was used to quantify insulin resistance. The homeostasis model assessment 
for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) was calculated as follows: HOMA-IR=serum glucose 
(mmol/L) × serum insulin (mU/L)/22.5.29 Fasting glucose and insulin levels of serum were 
determined in mice with their corresponding kits and expressed in mmol/L and mU/L, 
respectively.28, 30

Proteins extraction and Western blot analysis 
The expression of Nrf-2, ARE and PPARγ was determined by western blots.32 Briefly, the

PMSF and 20 mM NaF. Homogenates were centrifuged at 15000g, 4°C for 15 min. Protein

SDS-PAGE and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane (0.45 µm,

min for 3 cycles, the PVDF membranes were incubated overnight with primary specific

Histological observation 
Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and oil red O staining were used for the microscopic 
histological examination. Representative abdominal adipose tissue and liver samples from mice 
were fixed with 10% neutral formalin solution, and then the fixed tissues were embedded in 
paraffin, sectioned into 5-6 µm thickness, and stained with H&E dye. For oil red O staining, 
frozen liver sample were thawed on ice and then fixed and stained. The slides were detected 
under an Olympus light microscope for observations and photograph.33 Finally, the images were 
examined and evaluated for pathological change analysis. For the analysis, the relative 
vacuolated areas of liver tissues were calculated by the Image J 1.48 software (National 
Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA) and the adipocytes sizes were measured by Image J 
software with Adipocytes Tools plugins after pictures were recorded by light phase contrast 
microscopy. 
Statistical analysis 
All experiments were performed at least in triplicate and all results were expressed as means 
± SD (stander deviation). Statistical comparisons between groups were performed by one way 
analysis of variance with SPSS (v22.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA), followed by Tukey’s post 
hoc test. For all analysis, the p-values of ≤ 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

Table 1 showed the effects of HF diet and different dietary fiber supplementations on the 
body weights, food intake, liver weight and adipose tissue weight of the experimental C57BL/6J 
mice after 16 weeks of dietary intervention. During the experimental period, HF diet caused the 
decline of food intake as compared with the normal group (p<0.05), and food intake in the HF 
diet-fed mice supplemented with different DFs was also decreased as compared with that in HF 
feeding control (p<0.05). However, HF feeding showed an obvious increase in body weight gain, 
and the final body weight of HF-fed mice (45.94 ± 3.43 g) was significantly higher than that of 
the normal group mice (37.24 ± 1.68 g) after 16 weeks feeding, even though there was no 
significant difference in the initial body weight among all groups. Supplementation with BC, 
KGM and BC/KGM in HF-fed mice could significantly decrease body weight gain (p<0.05) in 
comparison with the HF control (Table 1). Meanwhile, the supplementations with different DFs, 
especially combined BC/KGM, could effectively decline the elevated liver and fat weight 
induced by HF diets (p<0.05), resulting in the low HI and abdominal fat rate. These results 
showed that dietary fibers could lower weight by decreasing liver weights and fat gain. 
DFs supplementation reduced glucose tolerance and insulin resistance 
To determine whether supplementation with different types of DFs in C57BL/6J mice could 
suppress systemic insulin resistance, the OGTT was performed at the termination of 16 week 
treatment. As shown in Fig. 1A, glucose concentrations of all animals peaked at time of 30 min 
after animals received a glucose load orally. HF-treated group displayed the highest glucose 
concentration during the period of OGTT study, while DFs supplementation reversed this 
change, where the combined BC/KGM showed excellent glucose-lowering effect in the 
experimental mice than single BC or KGM (Fig. 1A). Consistently, fasting glucose level in mice

group, relative to the normal group (p<0.05), while DFs significantly decreased HOMA-IR

especially the combined BC/KGM, could effectively meliorate the hyperglycemia and 
hyperinsulinemia induced by HF diet in mice. 
DFs supplementation ameliorated hepatic oxidant stress 
  To investigate whether supplement with BC, KGM and BC/KGM in HF diet could ameliorate 
hepatic oxidative stress, the hepatic activities of antioxidant enzymes including T-SOD, GSH-Px 
and CAT were determined. As depicted in Fig. 2A-C, hepatic T-SOD, GSH-Px and CAT 
activities of mice in HF-diet group were obviously decreased by approximately 33.5%, 51.0% 
and 25.7% in comparison with those in the normal group, respectively (p<0.05). As expected, 
the HF-caused decreases in hepatic activities of T-SOD, GSH-Px and CAT were effectively 
enhanced by DFs supplementation (p<0.05), indicating that HF intake for long term could cause 
hepatic oxidant injury and ingestion adequate DFs could inhibit those changes.

DFs ameliorated hepatic injury and normalized serum lipids levels 
Hepatic injury was evaluated by measuring serum ALP, ALT, AST and LDH levels, which 
were the indicators of leakage of hepatocytes into circulation under hepatotoxicity. As described 
in Table 2, serum ALP, ALT, AST and LDH levels in the HF-fed mice were obviously higher 
than those in the normal mice, suggesting that HF ingestion caused hepatic injury in C57BL/6J 
mice. However, supplementation with different DFs in HF-fed mice inhibited the elevation in 
the serum ALP, ALT, AST and LDH levels, and especially for the combined BC/KGM 
supplementation, the effects were better than single BC or KGM application (p<0.05). 
The serum lipid levels of TG, TC, LDL-C and HDL-C were shown in Table 2. Compared 
with the normal group, HF feeding in mice caused a significant increase in serum TG, TC, 
LDL-C and LDL-C/HDL-C levels, and a markedly decline in serum HDL-C (p<0.05),

DFs regulated the hepatic lipid metabolism and inflammatory cytokines 
To understand the effect of dietary fiber supplementation on hepatic lipid metabolism in mice, 
we next investigated activities of FAS and HL in the liver. As shown in Fig. 3A, the hepatic FAS 
level in the HF-fed mice was significantly higher than that in the normal mice, where the FAS 
activity was increased by 1.75-fold (p<0.05). However, hepatic FAS activity in mice 
supplemented with combined BC/KGM was effectively decreased by 53.3% (p<0.05), showing 
excellent FAS-lowering effect as compared with single BC (46.6%) or KGM (51.4%). In terms 
of hepatic HL levels, it was markedly decreased by 31.3% (p<0.05) in the HF group as 
compared with the normal group, while supplementation with BC, KGM and BC/KGM could 
effectively inhibit this decline in HL levels induced by HF diets (Fig. 3B, p<0.05), indicating 
that there was fat generation and accumulation in the liver, which might lead to hepatic oxidant 
stress and inflammatory response. Additionally, the levels of inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α 
and IL-6) were measured by ELISA assay. As described in Fig.3C and D, the secretion of TNF-α 
and IL-6 in the liver was markedly increased by 53.3% and 38.6% in HF-fed mice as compared 
with those in the normal mice, respectively (p<0.05). However, both single and mixed DFs 
supplementation displayed obvious prevention on the up-regulation of TNF-α and IL-6 in the

To further confirm the protective effects of DFs on HF-induced hepatic injury in C57BL/6J 
mice, histopathological morphologies of livers were observed using H&E and oil red O staining. 
As described in Fig. 4, clear hepatic cellular structures stained with H&E in the normal mice 
were observed, displaying no edema or hyperplasia in fibrous tissue (Fig. 4A). Nevertheless, HF 
feeding for consecutive 16 weeks caused severe hepatocyte necrosis, cytoplasmic vacuolation, 
and fragmentation of cell membrane and nuclear. Furthermore, the hepatic lobule structures in 
HF diet group were partly fuzzy, which was associated with inflammation (Fig. 4A), and the 
relative vacuolated areas were obviously increased which indicated a severe hepatic damage

Discussion 
Obesity has been a rapid increase in both developed and developing countries in the past 30 
years due to the unhealthful dietary habits (e.g. high fat diet or high-energy density diet) and 
lack of exercises,3, 6, 34 and some diseases, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, 
cancer and depression, are attributed to obesity.35, 36 Consequently, reduction of energy intake 
has been regarded as an effective way to control body weight gain by incorporation of some 
satiety ingredients (e.g. DFs) into diets.9, 11 In the present study, we are the first investigation 
with unequivocal evidence that the effect of DFs supplementation (BC, KGM and BC/KGM) on 
the C57BL/6J mice induced by HF diet. Results showed that supplementation with BC, KGM or 
combined BC/KGM efficiently lowered body weight, weight gain, liver weight and abdominal 
fat weight in comparison with those in the mice fed HF diet, especially the mixed BC/KGM 
supplementation (Table 1). Besides, the food intake of the C57BL/6J mice among the five 
experimental groups showed statistical difference, suggesting that the prevention of DFs against 
obesity was involved in the suppression of food intake and ingestion reduction of diet energy 
density. This effect was probably due to the high hydroscopicity of BC and KGM, which 
resulted in viscosity-producing effects and the satiety by delaying gastric empting.11, 13

Previous studies have found that insulin resistance can be reflected by a declined ability of 
insulin-mediated glucose transshipment to muscles and liver, and analysis of blood insulin has 
therefore been used to reflect insulin sensitivity in body.29, 37 The present results displayed that 
uptake of HF diet obviously caused an insulin resistance, in agreement with the previous 
studies.30, 38 However, the elevated blood glucose, insulin, and HOMA-IR were markedly 
prevented by DFs supplementation, especially the combined BC/KGM treatment, suggesting the 
beneficial effect of DFs on insulin sensitivity (Fig. 1). In addition, numerous studies have 
proved that insulin resistance status is well known to be highly associated with altered lipid 
profile (e.g. excess blood TG, TC, high and LDL-C/HDL-C levels).29, 39 Likewise, the present 
results showed that HF diet led to conspicuous dyslipidaemia in the experimental mice 
characterized by elevated levels of TC, TG, and LDL-C, and lowered levels of HDL-C (Table 2), 
which were in agreement with previous studies.38 These results indicated that the HF intake 
interfered with the lipid mechanism of the liver that might promote lipid deposition in 
hepatocytes and adipocytes, resulting in hyperlipidemia or fatty liver.38 However, the HF-fed 
mice supplemented with BC, KGM or a combination had a significant increase in HDL-C level 
and the drastic decreases in TC, TG and LDL-C levels. These results were consistent with the 
previous studies showing that DFs supplementation may improve the lipid profile in the serum 
and liver, suggesting that DFs ameliorate the lipid mechanism and lessen the lipid synthesis in 
mice. 23, 40 Furthermore, the oil red O staining of the liver tissues confirmed that DFs could 
normalize the HF-caused dyslipidemia and protect the liver from HF-induced histopathological 
alterations (Fig. 4), indicating that DFs, especially the combined BC/KGM fiber, inhibited the 
change in lipid mechanism caused by HF ingestion.

Evidence shows that fatty acid synthase (FAS) is associated with the synthesis of lipids and 
can catalyze the synthesis of triglycerides from de novo fatty acids synthesis. Futhermore, 
augmented FAS activity can cause excessive accumulation of lipids.41, 42 On the contrary,

containing VLDL and chylomicrons, thus leading to the release of free fatty acids and their 
subsequent uptake by myocytes for energy production or adipocytes for re-esterification and 
storage.43, 44 The present study demonstrated that the HF-caused increase in hepatic FAS activity 
and decline in HL activity could be effectively inhibited by supplementation with BC, KGM or 
combined BC/KGM (Fig. 3), indicating that the abnormal FAS and HL activities might lead to 
the lipid accumulation in the liver, and subsequently caused the oxidant stress. However, the 
liver in the DFs-treated mice showed scattered droplets of fat as compared to that in HF-fed 
mice (Fig. 4). 
LEP and ADPN are mainly secreted by adipocytes, and presented in adipose tissue or serum. 
The levels of LEP in adipose tissue and serum are related to fat mass in obesity. Besides, LEP is 
involved in the regulation of energy homeostasis and production of inflammatory cytokines.39, 45 
In the present work the level of LEP was associated with fat weights in abdominal tissues. 
ADPN has a negative correlation with obesity and an anti-inflammatory effect against TNF-α 
and IL-6.39 In our work, BC, KGM or combined BC/KGM ameliorated hepatic ADPN 
concentration of mice induced by HF diet (Fig. 5). These results suggested that the decrease in 
hepatic fat mass induced by DFs was associated with the increase in ADPN and decrease in LEP 
level, thus resulting in weight loss, which was in accordance with the previous studies39, 43 An 
imbalance between energy intake and expenditure could cause the increase of the number or size

KGM for functional dietary supplement against lipid-associated liver injury.
